scenes.narration: It works on my machine. Docker is how you stop saying that.
scenes.headline: “It works on my machine.”

set.headline: Your app, plus everything it needs, in one box

steps.say: It packs your app and everything it needs into one box, which runs the same on any computer.

scenes.title: Two ways to keep apps apart
scenes.narration: So it's a virtual machine? No.

steps.say: A virtual machine runs a whole operating system, kernel and all. A container is one walled off process that shares the host's kernel.
So many more of them fit on one machine.

scenes.narration: You describe the box in a Dockerfile.

steps.say: Start from a small image that has Node.
Install your packages, then copy in your code.
Say what to run, then build it.
steps.output:
$ docker build -t my-app .
 => [1/5] FROM docker.io/library/node:22-alpine
 => [2/5] WORKDIR /app
 => [3/5] COPY package*.json ./
 => [4/5] RUN npm install
 => [5/5] COPY . .
 => naming to docker.io/library/[my-app]{good}

scenes.title: The image, one layer per step
scenes.narration: That build makes an image: read only layers, one for each step, stacked on the base.

steps.say: Change your code, and only the top layer is built again. The rest come from the cache.

scenes.title: An image becomes a container
scenes.narration: Run the image, and you get a container.

steps.say: It starts in the background, port eighty eighty reaches the app inside, and it answers.

scenes.narration: The Dockerfile is the recipe. The image is what it builds. A container is that image, running, the same on every machine.
scenes.headline: Three words
items: **Dockerfile**: the recipe, one layer per step
**Image**: a read-only template built from it
**Container**: a running copy of an image
